fix: preserve Set-Cookie when Home Assistant ingress rewrites HTML

The HomeAssistant middleware rebuilds text/html responses to prefix static
and media URLs. It copied only response.headers into the new HttpResponse;
Django stores csrftoken and sessionid on response.cookies, so browsers
never received those cookies and CSRF/login failed behind ingress.

Copy response.cookies onto the rebuilt response (same pattern as add-on patch).

Closes #966
Refs #982

chore: reformat templates to satisfy djlint 1.42.x

The `lint` gulp task runs `djlint --check .`, and djlint is pinned as
`djlint = "~=1.0"` with no committed lockfile, so CI installs the latest
1.x at run time (currently 1.42.3). A recent 1.x release changed
template indentation rules, so `djlint --check .` now reports 13 existing
templates as needing reformatting — on master as well — which fails the
`test` job on every open PR regardless of its contents.

This applies `djlint --reformat` (formatting only; prettier already
ignores `*.html`, and no Python changed) to make `djlint --check .`
green again. If you'd rather freeze formatting instead, pinning djlint
to the previously-used version is an equally valid fix — happy to switch.
chore: update formatting for djlint changes

chore(deps): allow django-imagekit >=6.0 (fix 500 on Python 3.14) (#1104)

On Python 3.14 every page that renders a child thumbnail raises
`TypeError: _Pickler._batch_setitems() missing 1 required positional
argument: 'obj'` from imagekit/hashers.py. Python 3.14 changed the
private pickle API to `_batch_setitems(self, items, obj)`; django-imagekit
5.0.0 calls it with a single argument.

The fix shipped in django-imagekit 6.0 (matthewwithanm/django-imagekit#583),
but the `~=5.0` pin excludes it. Bump the constraint to `~=6.0` and pin
6.1.0 in requirements.txt. imagekit 6.1.0 supports Python 3.9-3.14 and
requires only django-appconf and pilkit, both already pinned (pilkit==3.0
unchanged), so no other dependencies change.

Fixes #1103.

test(core): cover timer update message with no child

TimerFormsTestCase.test_edit already edits a childless timer, but only
asserts on the name and start time, so the success message was never
covered. Editing such a timer currently renders "Timer entry for None
updated."

Committed ahead of the fix so the history shows the defect before it is
resolved.

Committed with --no-verify. The pre-commit hook runs `gulp lint`, which
spawns `npx` through Node's spawn() without a shell; on Windows `npx` is
`npx.cmd`, which spawn cannot execute, so the hook fails with
"spawn npx ENOENT" before checking anything. Ran the checks covering this
change manually instead: `black --check` clean across 192 files, and
`djlint --check` clean. Prettier does not process Python files.

Refs #922

fix(core): omit child from timer update message when unset

CoreUpdateView.get_success_message tested `"child" in cleaned_data`,
which checks that the key exists rather than that it holds a value.
Timer.child is the only optional child foreign key in the project
(blank=True, null=True) and TimerForm includes the field, so editing a
timer with no child took the "for %(child)s" branch and interpolated
None.

Checking the value instead selects the existing fallback string,
"%(model)s entry updated.", which is already translated in every locale.
No new translatable string is introduced.

CoreAddView carries the same pattern but is left alone: TimerAdd does not
inherit from it, and no other model allows a null child, so it cannot be
reached with one.

Committed with --no-verify for the same Windows tooling reason given in
the preceding commit. `black --check` is clean on this file.

chore: create v2.10.1 release

feat: add a scoped caregiver user role

Adds a `caregiver` group for babysitters and other temporary carers,
following the existing `read_only` group pattern rather than a new
token or grant system.

A caregiver may view children, timers, feedings, diaper changes and
sleep entries, and add and edit feedings, diaper changes, sleep
entries and timers, through both the web interface and the API. A
caregiver may not delete anything, cannot reach medication,
temperature, growth data, notes, pumping or tummy time, and cannot
manage users, change site settings or open the database admin area.

- `BABY_BUDDY["CAREGIVER_GROUP_NAME"]` setting and group creation
- `post_migrate` permission sync alongside the read-only one
- `is_caregiver` checkbox on the user form, mutually exclusive with
  `is_read_only`
- `manage.py createuser --caregiver`
- "Caregiver" column on the user list, via a `user_is_caregiver` tag
- Documentation, including the limits of the role

The role is a set of model permissions and nothing more: it applies to
every child on the instance, it does not expire, and Baby Buddy does
not record which user created an entry, so a caregiver's entries
cannot be told apart from anyone else's afterwards. The documentation
says so explicitly and points at deactivating the user as the way to
withdraw access, which does take effect immediately, including for an
API key already handed out.

No migration is required; the group and its permissions are created by
the existing `post_migrate` receivers.

feat: widen the caregiver scope and make its permissions adjustable

Follows the review on #1134. A caregiver is looking after a child, so the
models they may record are widened to include medication, temperature,
weight, notes and tummy time, alongside the existing feedings, diaper
changes, sleep and timers. The model is rigid — a permission is
instance-wide and the group is the only role — so erring on the side of
more access is the safer default.

What stays out is what a caregiver has no reason to record: pumping, the
growth measurements tracked over months (height, BMI, head circumference),
and everything administrative (children, tags, users, sites). `delete` is
never granted.

The group stays a default rather than a fixed role. A caregiver is an
ordinary Django user, so individual permissions can be granted on top of it
from the database admin area, where Django's permission picker already
lives. Django has no per-user deny, so this is additive only, and the
documentation says so instead of promising a granularity that does not
exist.

fix(core): populate the read-only group on first migrate

`add_read_only_group_permissions` was connected to `post_migrate` with
`sender=self`, so it ran once, on `core`'s own signal — before either
of the things it depends on exists:

- `core`'s permissions are created by `django.contrib.auth`, which is
  listed after `core` in `INSTALLED_APPS`, so its receiver runs later;
- the group itself is created on `babybuddy`'s signal, also later.

The receiver found neither and returned without doing anything: a
fresh install left `read_only` with no permissions, and read-only users
could not view any data until a second `migrate` happened to run.

Dropping the sender filter runs the receiver on every application's
signal, which converges on the complete set. `Group.permissions.add()`
is idempotent, so the repeats are harmless, and a `dispatch_uid`
guards against double registration.

Verified against a fresh SQLite database: 0 permissions after the first
`migrate` before this change, 18 after; 18 after the first with it.

fix: apply model permissions to reports, the timeline and dashboard cards

Three places read core models without checking whether the user may
see them. Standard users are superusers and read-only users hold every
`view` permission, so this is invisible on a stock install — but a
narrower role runs straight into it.

- Reports were gated on `core.view_child` alone, so that one permission
  opened the weight, height, BMI, head circumference, medication,
  temperature, pumping and tummy time reports. Each report now also
  requires the `view` permission of the model it renders, and the index
  only links to the reports the user can open.
- `timeline.get_objects()` always added medication, note, temperature
  and tummy time events. It now takes the user the timeline is rendered
  for and leaves out the event types they have no `view` permission
  for. Passing no user keeps the previous behaviour.
- The child dashboard rendered every card unconditionally. Cards are
  now guarded by the permission of the model they read, and the
  statistics card, which spans several models, filters each section
  individually.

Adds tests for all three with a user holding only the child, timer,
feeding, diaper change and sleep `view` permissions, plus read-only
cases so the existing behaviour stays covered.

fix: correct the permission codenames used by head circumference and tags

Django returns `False` from `has_perm()` and from the `{% if perms.x.y %}`
template tag for a permission that does not exist, rather than raising. A
codename that does not match the one Django creates therefore denies access
to every user who holds the correct permission, with no error to explain it.

`HeadCircumference` declares `model_name = "head_circumference"`, but Django
derives permission codenames from the model class name and not from
`model_name`, so the four permissions are `*_headcircumference`. The views
and templates asked for `*_head_circumference` instead, which never exists.
`Tag` generates `view_tag`, while the two tag views asked for `view_tags`.

The effect was measurable: a user holding all four head circumference
permissions, or `core.view_tag`, received 403 on `/head-circumference/`,
`/head-circumference/add/` and `/tags/`. The read-only group was unaffected
because it builds its permission list from `apps.all_models`, which yields
the correct codenames, so this only ever broke users and groups that were
granted permissions explicitly, for example through the admin permission
picker.

The tests fail with that same 403 against the previous code, and also assert
that no view or template refers to a `core.*` permission that does not exist,
so a future typo is caught even on a code path no request exercises.

fix: stop the password reset test from logging out the shared client

`ViewsTestCase` logs in once in `setUpClass` and shares that client (`cls.c`)
across every test in the class. `test_password_reset` called `self.c.logout()`
on it, so whichever tests ran afterwards inherited a logged-out client.

Django orders tests alphabetically within a class, so `test_password_reset`
runs before `test_rolling_sessions`, `test_root_router`, `test_user_settings`,
`test_user_unlock`, `test_user_views` and `test_welcome` -- exactly the six
that failed:

    AssertionError: '/login/?next=/' != '/dashboard/'
    AssertionError: 302 != 200
    AssertionError: 302 != 403
    AssertionError: 'Set-Cookie: sessionid=""...' == 'Set-Cookie: sessionid=""...'

The test carried an `isolate` tag, which the test runner turns into
`--exclude-tag isolate` plus a separate run for the tagged test alone. That
worked around the symptom but kept the cause: the whole suite only passed when
invoked with the runner's flags, and `manage.py test` without them reported six
failures that looked like real regressions and were not.

The test now takes its own client instead of logging out the shared one. That
covers only this test: the task in `#148` that added the tag was about running
a test by itself, whereas the actual coupling here is one test mutating state
seven other tests depend on, which a separate client fixes at the source.

Verified four ways, all green:
- the runner's invocation, `--parallel --exclude-tag isolate`: 331 tests OK
- `manage.py test` with no flags at all (previously 6 failures): 331 tests OK
- `ViewsTestCase` alone: 10 tests OK
- `test_password_reset` alone: 1 test OK

The `isolate` tag and the gulp wiring for it are left in place: nothing uses
the tag any more, but removing that infrastructure means touching the parallel
and coverage-combining steps in `gulpfile.js`, which is a separate decision.

Consuming a timer deletes it, so both the form and the API serializer now
require `core.delete_timer` before a timer can be used to record an entry,
for the caller's own timers too. The timer is locked and stopped only after
the entry and its tags have saved, inside one transaction, so a failed save
leaves it in place.

Tag assignment on an entry is now gated as well: `core.change_tag` to change
which tags are attached, `core.add_tag` additionally for names that do not
exist yet. Unchanged resubmissions stay valid and omitted tags are preserved.

Removing the tag widget for users without `core.change_tag` had also replaced
it with a plain hidden input, which rendered tags as object representations
instead of names. That value was posted back on an ordinary edit and refused,
so a caregiver could not correct their own tagged entry. The substitute input
formats tag names again.

Also rejects Caregiver + Staff in the user form and `createuser`, scopes the
default permission lookup to the `core` app, and updates the user guide to
describe the live group sync, the full care scope and the timer and tag
permission requirements.

feat: add notes field to Tummy Time

TummyTime is the only care entry model without a notes field, while BMI,
DiaperChange, Feeding, HeadCircumference, Height, Medication, Pumping,
Sleep, Temperature and Weight all have one. This makes Tummy Time entries
unable to carry free form notes alongside the milestone.

Add the field on the model, expose it in the form, the API serializer and
the list template, and regenerate the part of the OpenAPI schema that
covers TummyTime.

The notes row in the list template follows the same pattern as the other
list views: a details row below the entry, rendered only when notes are
present. The colspan of both that row and the empty state row now take
the optional child column into account, which the empty state row
previously did not.

feat: let users complete their own timers

* feat: let users complete their own timers

Converting a timer into an entry deletes the timer, so it required
`core.delete_timer`, even for the user who started it. The owner of a timer
may now convert it into an entry. Converting another user's timer still
requires `core.delete_timer`.

Because owning a timer now carries that right, ownership no longer changes
as a side effect. Editing a timer in the web interface kept assigning it to
the editor, and a partial update through the API without `user` did the same.
Both now keep the existing owner, and changing the user of an existing timer
through the API requires `core.delete_timer`.

* fix: recheck timer ownership once the timer is locked

The owner check ran during validation, before the timer row was locked, so
a timer reassigned in between could still be converted by its former owner.
Converting a timer now checks again on the locked row, in the API and in the
web forms.

Updating a timer through the API now works on the locked, stored timer, so a
change of owner made in the meantime is checked and never overwritten with
the stale value. Editing a timer in the web interface saves only the form's
fields, for the same reason.

feat: add an optional access expiry to user accounts

* feat: add an optional access expiry to user accounts

A user can now be given an "Access expires" time in the user form, for
example for a babysitter who only needs access for a weekend. Once it has
passed, the user is signed out and can no longer sign in or use the API,
including with an existing API key.

The account is not deactivated: moving or clearing the time restores access.
The expiry is stored in the user's settings but is not part of the settings
form, so users cannot change their own.

Web sessions are checked in a view hook so that users signed in through
`REVERSE_PROXY_AUTH` are covered too. API tokens are checked in a
`TokenAuthentication` subclass.

* fix: say that access has expired in the API error

An expired account is neither inactive nor deleted. The API now answers with
the same message as the web interface.

feat(core): show the timer name on activity add forms

* feat(core): show the timer name on activity forms

When an entry is added from a timer, the add form is pre-filled with the
timer's start time but the timer name is not shown anywhere, which makes
it hard to tell which timer is being finished. Add a read-only Timer
field right after the Child field with the timer title.

* fix(core): handle invalid timer ids defensively

An add form opened with an invalid `?timer=<id>` keeps the id around, so
submitting the form raised `Timer.DoesNotExist` and returned a 500. Only
stop the timer when it still exists, and make the field helper a no-op when
the item is missing or already at the anchor.
